evidence: The record itself is the evidence: 'B.B.E. (Big Booty Express)' on Welcome 2 Detroit (BBE, 2001), credited to Jay Dee, interpolates the vocal hook of Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' and is otherwise an original composition. Its framing as a tribute to Detroit's absorption of Kraftwerk is the label's and critics' reading and is not documented from Dilla himself.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen to how Kraftwerk say the title: flat, chanted, treated voices over a clanking rhythm meant to sound like a train. Then listen to how Dilla's track keeps the shape and rhythm of that chant and swaps the words, so the hook is instantly familiar and slightly ridiculous. Underneath, the music is his, not a sample of theirs. It is a Detroit hip-hop producer quoting the record Detroit's techno producers learned from.

explanation: Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' was a big influence on Detroit, where DJs played it and techno producers learned from it. J Dilla grew up in Detroit, and on his 2001 album he borrowed its chanted hook, changing the words to 'Big Booty Express', and made the rest of the music himself: a joke and a salute to his city's musical history at the same time. It crosses lineages, and it is the one connection on this map so far between Detroit hip-hop and the Kraftwerk-to-techno line it grew up next to, through Atkins and May. It is documented as a borrowing because the record carries it. The wider claim that Dilla's rhythm owes anything to Detroit techno is not made here, because nothing consulted supports it.
